headline: RBA warns inflation is getting worse, oil spikes above $99, and the ASX slipped 0.43% — a mixed day across your portfolio with Google the biggest drag from last night's session.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google slipped 1.62% last night after CEO Sundar Pichai revealed that Google Cloud is deliberately giving up revenue to build out AI capacity — a short-term earnings headwind that spooked investors even as the broader NASDAQ rallied 1%. Earnings are due in about a week, so markets are watching closely.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara dropped another 2.06% today as lithium sentiment remains weak. China's Tianqi Lithium reported Q3 earnings slumped over 25% quarter-on-quarter, a sign the lithium price recovery is still fragile. The long-term demand story (BNEF forecasts 4.8 million tonnes of lithium demand by 2050) remains intact, but the near-term pressure is real.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE fell 1.42% today, the worst of the Vanguard ETFs. Emerging markets are feeling the pinch from a stronger US dollar, rising oil prices (now near $100/barrel) which hurts oil-importing developing economies, and lingering Middle East tension.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI dipped 1.09% on the ASX today, which is a bit surprising given the NASDAQ AI rebound last night. The ASX AI ETF tends to lag US moves by a day, so today's session was likely catching up to earlier weakness rather than reflecting last night's positive session.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft edged up 0.2% last night and held steady while the broader NASDAQ rallied. Earnings are due 28 October — analysts expect the stock could move around 4.6% either way on the result. The AI story around Azure cloud continues to be the key focus for investors.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two barely moved last night, down just 0.26%. GTA 6 launch preparation content is circulating online, keeping the title in the news cycle — a reminder of the major catalyst coming for this stock when the game eventually hits shelves.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped a modest 0.34% today, broadly in line with the ASX 200's 0.43% fall. Nothing specific to worry about — this is just the fund tracking global markets on a slightly soft day.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped 0.34% on the ASX today, but this reflects yesterday's US session rather than last night's NASDAQ rally (which was up 1.05%). Expect VTS to potentially recover when it prices in last night's strong US session tomorrow.

movers.name: BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF
movers.note: DHHF barely moved, down 0.24% — essentially flat. A quiet, uneventful session for this broad diversified holding.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike risk rising — watch your borrowing costs
watch_today.detail: The RBA's deputy governor warned today that the inflation outlook is 'materially worse', and markets are now pricing a real chance of a fifth interest rate hike this year, with traders floating the idea of the cash rate going above 5%. This matters directly: higher rates mean higher mortgage repayments, tighter household budgets, and usually pressure on growth stocks and property. Keep an eye on the RBA's next meeting.

watch_today.title: MSFT earnings on 28 October — key moment for your holding
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reports earnings next Tuesday 28 October (US time). Analysts expect the stock could swing around 4.6% either way. The key question is whether Azure cloud AI growth is accelerating. You're up 20% on this position overall — no reason to sell before earnings, but be ready for some volatility next week.

watch_today.title: GOOG — down last night but earnings due soon, sit tight
watch_today.detail: Google fell 1.62% last night after Pichai confirmed Google Cloud is trading short-term revenue for AI infrastructure buildout. Earnings are due in about a week. You're still up 7.65% overall on this small position. The long-term AI and cloud story is intact — this is not the time to panic. Hold and see what earnings reveal.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — lithium pain continues, long-term thesis still intact
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped another 2% today and you're down 57.7% overall on this position. The short-term picture is genuinely tough — Chinese lithium earnings are sliding and spot prices remain depressed. However, BNEF's long-term forecast of 4.8 million tonnes demand by 2050 hasn't changed. This is a stock to hold (or consider topping up at these levels if you believe in the EV story) — selling now locks in a big loss at the worst point of the cycle.

watch_today.title: Oil surging past $99 — watch inflation and emerging markets
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) jumped 2.39% last night to nearly $100/barrel. This feeds directly into inflation — higher fuel costs push up prices across the economy, making the RBA's job harder and increasing the chance of another rate hike. It also hurts your VGE (emerging markets ETF), since many developing countries are oil importers.

watch_today.title: VTS.AX — dipped today but US markets rallied last night
watch_today.detail: VTS fell 0.34% on the ASX today, but this was pricing in an earlier US session. Last night the NASDAQ rose 1.05% and the S&P 500 gained 0.58%. VTS should reflect some of that strength tomorrow. Nothing to do here — your long-term US market exposure is working exactly as intended.

world.summary: Middle East tensions are escalating sharply, with the US ordering diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi missile strikes. US-Canada relations are strained over election interference allegations, and US domestic politics is heating up ahead of the midterms. Meanwhile, the IMF is warning of global economic risks.

stories.title: US orders diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi strikes hit Dammam airport
stories.why_it_matters: The US has ordered its diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia after Houthi forces — the Iran-backed group based in Yemen — launched a missile strike on Dammam airport in Saudi Arabia, killing one person. This is a major escalation: Houthi attacks on Saudi soil are rare and deeply destabilising. The US pulling diplomats out signals Washington believes the risk of further strikes is high. For everyday Australians, the direct concern is oil — Saudi Arabia is one of the world's biggest producers, and any serious disruption to its operations could push oil prices (already near $100/barrel) significantly higher, meaning more expensive fuel and higher inflation.

stories.title: US-Canada tensions flare over midterm election interference claims
stories.why_it_matters: The US Embassy in Ottawa has publicly accused Canada's Carney government of brushing off American concerns about 'potential interference' in the upcoming US midterm elections. Multiple news outlets report that Democrat-aligned state attorneys general are also ramping up legal action to block Trump's administration from meddling in how states run their elections. This unusual public spat between two close allies signals just how fractured and fraught the US political environment has become. It also raises questions about the integrity of the November midterms, which will determine whether Trump's party controls Congress.

stories.title: State attorneys general sue to block Trump's election interference
stories.why_it_matters: Democratic state attorneys general across the US are suing the Trump administration to stop it from overriding states' authority to run their own elections ahead of the November midterms. The legal battle centres on a Trump executive order that critics say gives the federal government unprecedented power over election administration — something the Constitution traditionally leaves to states. This is shaping up to be a major constitutional fight that could affect how tens of millions of Americans vote in just weeks.

stories.title: Middle East oil exports climbing back to pre-war levels
stories.why_it_matters: Despite ongoing conflict in the Middle East, the Financial Times reports that oil exports from the region are recovering back to pre-war levels. This is partly why global oil markets had remained relatively stable — until now. With Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia escalating and the US pulling diplomats, that export recovery could be threatened, helping to explain why crude oil jumped nearly 2.4% last night to almost $100 a barrel.

stories.title: IMF warns of global economic risks that could deepen cost-of-living pressure
stories.why_it_matters: The International Monetary Fund has issued a fresh warning about global economic risks, noting that a combination of geopolitical tensions, sticky inflation, and high interest rates could deepen cost-of-living pressures worldwide. For Australians, this is relevant context: our own RBA is already warning inflation is getting worse, and a global slowdown would hurt export demand (especially for commodities like lithium and iron ore) while keeping local rates elevated.

markets.summary: Last night was a tale of two markets — Wall Street had a decent session with the NASDAQ up over 1% on AI stock strength, while today the ASX slipped 0.43% as the RBA's inflation warning weighed on sentiment. Oil is the big story, surging nearly 2.4% to nearly $100/barrel on Middle East escalation. Gold eased slightly.

indicators.note: Fell today as RBA inflation warnings dampened mood

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Strong last night, led by AI and tech earnings optimism

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Surging on Houthi strikes against Saudi Arabia — near $100

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Eased slightly as risk appetite improved on Wall Street

indicators.note: Aussie dollar holding above 70 US cents

politics.summary: The RBA has fired a warning shot on inflation, with its deputy governor saying the outlook is 'materially worse' — raising the real prospect of a fifth interest rate hike this year. Financial markets and economists are scrambling to reassess, with some now putting odds on the cash rate going above 5%.

stories.title: RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' — fifth rate hike odds shorten sharply
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank's deputy governor has openly warned that Australia's inflation outlook has become 'materially worse', shocking markets that had hoped rate rises were done. Traders are now pricing in a real probability of a fifth rate hike this year, with the AFR reporting some market participants are now pricing in a cash rate above 5% (it currently sits at 4.85%). For everyday Aussies, this means mortgage repayments could rise again, and the relief many were expecting from rate cuts next year looks further away. The RBA's next board meeting will be watched very closely.

stories.title: Treasurer Chalmers under pressure to act as RBA carries the inflation-fighting load
stories.why_it_matters: With the RBA again raising alarm bells about inflation, commentary is growing that Treasurer Jim Chalmers needs to take a more active role in reducing demand in the economy — rather than leaving it all to interest rate rises. The argument is that fiscal policy (government spending and taxation) should be doing more of the heavy lifting, rather than forcing the RBA to keep hiking rates and squeezing mortgage holders. It's a debate that will likely intensify if another rate rise comes.

ai.summary: The AI model wars are heating up, with a new benchmark comparison showing a 15x performance gap between leading models. DeepSeek launched a new product pressing OpenAI and Anthropic, and there's growing debate globally about whether AI companies should be regulated or trusted to self-regulate.

stories.title: Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 vs Gemini 4 Argon — benchmark shows 15x performance gap between AI leaders
stories.why_it_matters: A new head-to-head benchmark comparison of the three leading AI models — Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, OpenAI's GPT-6.1, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon — reportedly shows a 15x performance gap between the best and worst performers on complex tasks. This kind of gap matters because it signals that AI capability differences are no longer marginal — one model can be dramatically more useful than another depending on what you're asking it to do. It's also relevant for your GOOG holding: Google's Gemini needs to be competitive here.

stories.title: DeepSeek launches DeepInfer, taking direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic
stories.why_it_matters: China's DeepSeek — which stunned the AI world earlier this year with a highly capable, low-cost model — has now launched 'DeepInfer', a new product that takes direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic's commercial offerings. DeepSeek has shown a pattern of releasing models that match Western rivals at a fraction of the cost, which puts competitive pressure on all the big US AI players including Google (your GOOG holding) and Microsoft (your MSFT holding). More competition from China means these companies need to keep innovating fast.

stories.title: OpenAI president calls for AI safeguards — while funding a group that opposes AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI's president Greg Brockman has publicly called for stronger AI safety safeguards — but Reuters reveals he's simultaneously funding a lobbying group that actively opposes AI regulation. This contradiction highlights a broader tension in the AI industry: companies publicly embrace safety while quietly resisting rules that might slow them down. It's fuelling a growing debate in governments worldwide (including India and the US) about whether self-regulation can be trusted, or whether binding laws are needed.

stories.title: Unstructured's new AI models beat GPT-6, Claude and Gemini at reading documents, tables and scans
stories.why_it_matters: A startup called Unstructured has released specialised AI models that outperform the big names — GPT-6, Claude, and Gemini — specifically at reading and extracting information from messy documents like scanned forms, tables, and PDFs. This is the kind of unglamorous but incredibly valuable task that businesses actually need AI for. It shows that smaller, specialised AI players can carve out significant advantages over the tech giants in specific real-world applications — a reminder that not all AI value will flow to the biggest companies.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done and dusted — Roosters beat the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. The AFL draft season is heating up, and there's plenty of NRL player movement news flying around ahead of the off-season.

stories.title: Roosters win the 2026 NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights — one of the great finishes
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters are the 2026 NRL premiers, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a heart-stopping Grand Final at Accor Stadium. A one-point margin — it doesn't get much tighter than that. It's a massive moment for the Roosters club and a gutting loss for Newcastle, who came agonisingly close to their first premiership in years.

stories.title: PNG Chiefs unveil first logo and jersey in 'watershed' moment for NRL expansion
stories.why_it_matters: The Papua New Guinea Chiefs have officially revealed their inaugural logo and jersey as they prepare to join the NRL competition. Fox Sports is calling it a 'watershed' moment for the game. PNG is a rugby league-mad nation and having their own NRL team is a massive deal for the sport's growth across the Pacific.

stories.title: Titans target two Queensland Origin stars; Storm gun linked to shock club — Transfer Whispers
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL player market is buzzing post-Grand Final with the Gold Coast Titans reportedly chasing two Queensland Origin players in a potential swap deal. Separately, a Melbourne Storm gun is being linked with a surprise move to a rival club. The off-season silly season is well and truly underway — worth watching if you follow the Titans locally.

stories.title: AFL 2026 draft heating up — top rucks and tall forwards ranked
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL has released its latest draft prospect rankings with a focus on rucks and tall forwards ahead of the 2026 National Draft. AFL analyst Kevin Sheehan has named his top prospects in those key positions. With the Swans also facing a major captaincy decision — reportedly with five clubs also weighing leadership changes — the AFL off-season is setting up to be fascinating for fans of any club.
